item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q021_nad_binding_convergent_evolution","answer":"NAD(P) binding in multiple SCOP folds and superfamilies indicates that the ability to bind the same dinucleotide cofactor has evolved independently multiple times: similar chemistry and steric constraints can produce convergent phosphate/ribose-binding motifs and active-site geometries in otherwise unrelated proteins. Divergent evolution is supported within a SCOP family (clearer homology) or superfamily (probable common ancestry), but sharing a fold alone is weaker evidence; occurrence in different folds generally argues against whole-domain homology. Cofactor identity, a short glycine-rich motif, or a few similarly positioned catalytic residues can arise convergently and therefore cannot establish ancestry or justify transferring substrate specificity, reaction mechanism, or functional annotation. Homology requires broader evidence such as significant sequence/profile similarity across the domain, compatible overall topology and structural-core alignment, conserved residue patterns beyond the ligand-binding site, and phylogenetic support. Likewise, a structural template or representative should be chosen using domain-wide family/superfamily relationships and relevant functional context, not merely NAD versus NADP binding or local active-site resemblance.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
